newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-ENGLISH LEAGUE TOLD TO EXPAND AND MODERNISE.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-ENGLISH LEAGUE TOLD TO EXPAND AND MODERNISE.

text.p: The English Football League was told on Tuesday it would "wither on the vine" if it failed to expand, reform and modernise to meet the demands of soccer in the 21st century. And a consultant who has studied the organisation said: "Over the next five years 20 League clubs will face serious financial problems and could go bust if nothing is done to reform it."

London-based management consultants Deloitte and Touche, who have just completed an extensive study into the way the world's oldest competitive league, which began in 1888, is organised, concluded the League needed a massive overhaul.
"The need for change comes through from absolutely everybody we've spoken too," one of the report's authors Gerry Boon told a news conference.
"The League's image is very low... The whole organisation has to be turned on its head. It has to be market-led and not administration-driven.
"There really is no standstill option. The view coming through from the clubs is that the Football League is withering on the vine."

The English League started with 12 clubs in 1888 and although there are 92 first-class clubs in England, 20 elite clubs now play in the Premier League, formed five years to maximize profits from TV rights and other revenue.
The actual Football League -- the English league's official title -- itself now comprises 72 clubs in three national divisions.

The study, commissioned by the Football League in January, said the lowest division of the three tier league -- which excludes the lucrative premier league -- should be split in two along geographical lines.
The lower divisions were regionalised between 1921 and 1958 when a Third Division South and Third Division North operated. They became a nationwide Division Three and Division Four in 1958.
The new regional divisions, "north" and "south", should be bolstered by the addition of 16 semi-professional clubs currently playing in the minor leagues, the study said.
This would mean cash-strapped clubs would not have to travel long distances for matches and gate receipts would be boosted by an increase in local derbies.
Similar regional divisions operate in the leagues in France, Italy and Germany.
Deloitte and Touche said this reform alone would generate around 50,000 extra pounds ($81,000) per club per year.
Boon also recommended an increase in the number of promotion and relegation places to make the league more fluid.

"At the moment, the dream of bridging the gap between the Football League and the premier league is just that -- a dream," he said. "More relegation and promotion places would give clubs a realistic and achievable level of aspiration."
He said it would also help sustain interest among fans of mid-table clubs right through until the end of the season.
"At the moment, from February or early March onwards about half the teams in each division have nothing to play for," Boon said. "The league has to minimise meaningless matches."
Deloitte and Touche said the League could implement the changes recommended in the report by the start of the 1998-99 season if the 72 clubs involved agreed.
And the company warned of the consequences if the League clubs ignored the study's findings.
"Our expert opinion, and the opinion of many people we consulted, is that this really is the last chance.
"The old management committee style has to go if the Football League is to be successful in the future. This is a 40 million pound ($64 million) business and it has to be run as such."
The League described the report as "probably the most wide-ranging on the state of our national game that has ever been conducted."
But it said it could not comment on its findings until it had been fully debated by the League's 72 club chairmen. That debate is due to take place on Thursday.
The chairmen will vote on the recommendations at the League annual general meeting in June.
Asked whether he thought the chairmen would approve the far-reaching measures, Boon said: "I hope they do, I'm willing them to do it."
